title: Layers, encapsulation and devices
subtitle: A network is a stack of small promises: each layer uses the one below and offers a simpler service to the one above.

sections.title: Why layers
sections.body:
Think of sending a parcel abroad. You do not drive it to the other country yourself; you hand it to a clerk, who hands it to a courier, who hands it to a pilot. Each person does one job and trusts the next. Networks work the same way, and you should see why. Sending a web page across the world involves electrical signals, error checking, finding a route, making delivery reliable and speaking HTTP. Nobody builds that as one program.

A layered architecture splits the job: each layer talks to the same layer on the other machine through a protocol, and uses only the service of the layer beneath it. Layers can be replaced independently, Wi-Fi for Ethernet, without touching the layers above. The OSI model has seven layers (physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application); the TCP/IP model that the Internet actually uses has four: link, internet, transport, application. TCP/IP folds layers 5–7 into “application” and 1–2 into “link”. Which layer is responsible for end-to-end delivery between processes? The transport layer.

questions.prompt: Which layer is responsible for end-to-end delivery between processes?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It addresses hosts and finds routes, not processes.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: IP moves packets between hosts; transport (TCP/UDP) connects a process on one host to a process on the other using port numbers.

figures.caption: Figure 1.1.1 — the OSI stack
figures.note: TCP/IP folds layers 5–7 into “application” and 1–2 into “link”.

group "OSI" { o7, o6, o5, o4, o3, o2, o1 }

keynotes: A layered architecture splits the job: each layer talks to the same layer on the other machine through a protocol and uses only the service of the layer beneath.
Layers can be replaced independently, such as Wi-Fi for Ethernet, without touching the layers above.
The OSI model has seven layers; the TCP/IP model the Internet uses has four: link, internet, transport, application.

sections.title: Encapsulation
sections.body:
Imagine putting a letter in an envelope, then that envelope in a bigger envelope, and so on. Each layer adds its own wrapper, and you can picture the stack as a set of nesting envelopes. Going down the stack each layer adds its own header (the data link layer also a trailer) around what it was given. The application data becomes a TCP segment, then an IP packet, then an Ethernet frame, then bits. The receiver peels the headers off in reverse. Each header carries exactly what that layer needs: ports, IP addresses, MAC addresses.

Count the cost. A 1000-byte application message goes through TCP (20-byte header), IP (20) and Ethernet (14 + 4 trailer). The frame size = 1000 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 = 1058 bytes, and the overhead fraction is 58/1058 ≈ 5.5%. Press Simulate to watch the headers accumulate. Going down, the headers are added in the order TCP, then IP, then Ethernet.

worked.why: A 1000-byte application message goes through TCP (20-byte header), IP (20) and Ethernet (14 + 4 trailer).

questions.prompt: In which order are headers added as data travels down the stack?

choices.text: Transport, then network, then data link.
All at once by the application.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is the order they are removed at the receiver.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each layer wraps what it receives from above, so the lowest layer’s header ends up outermost.

figures.note: Press Simulate to watch the headers accumulate.

keynotes: Going down the stack each layer adds its own header (the data link layer also a trailer): TCP segment, IP packet, Ethernet frame, then bits.
The receiver peels the headers off in reverse; each header carries what that layer needs: ports, IP addresses, MAC addresses.
A 1000-byte message with TCP (20), IP (20) and Ethernet (14 + 4) headers becomes a 1058-byte frame, an overhead of about 5.5%.

sections.title: Networks and topologies
sections.body:
Networks come in sizes and shapes, and you have probably used all of them. A LAN covers a building, a MAN a city, and a WAN a country or more. Their topologies, the pattern of connections, matter too: bus (one shared cable), star (all to a central switch, the modern LAN), ring, and mesh (many links, resilient).

Who provides the service? In a client–server network servers provide services; in peer-to-peer every host is both. Why do modern LANs use a star rather than a bus? Because if one cable breaks only one machine is cut off, instead of the whole network.

questions.prompt: Why do modern LANs use a star rather than a bus?

choices.text: A fault in one cable affects one host, and a switch gives each link its own bandwidth.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: They cost money; the benefit is isolation.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: On a bus a single break or collision disturbs everyone.

keynotes: A LAN covers a building, a MAN a city and a WAN a country or more.
Topologies are bus (one shared cable), star (all to a central switch, the modern LAN), ring and mesh (many links, resilient).
In client–server networks servers provide services; in peer-to-peer every host is both.

sections.title: Devices by layer
sections.body:
Each box in a network lives at a particular layer, as you will see, and the higher the layer, the smarter the box. A repeater or hub regenerates bits (layer 1), floods every port, and forms one collision domain. A bridge or switch forwards frames by MAC address (layer 2), learning which address lives on which port. A router forwards packets between networks by IP address (layer 3). A gateway translates between different protocol stacks, often at the application layer.

Each step up the layers sees more of the packet. A switch receives a frame for a MAC address it has not seen before: what does it do? It floods the frame out of every port except the one it came in on, and learns as the replies return.

questions.prompt: A switch receives a frame for a MAC address it has not seen before. What does it do?

choices.text: Floods it out of every port except the one it came from, then learns the sender’s port.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That would make a new host unreachable.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Once the destination replies, the switch knows its port.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Switches do not reason about IP.

[Switch: layer 2, by MAC] as s #violet
[Router: layer 3, by IP] as r #amber

h -> s
s -> r
r -> g");

A bridge or switch forwards frames by MAC address (layer 2), learning which address lives on which port; a router forwards packets between networks by IP address (layer 3).
A gateway translates between different protocol stacks, often at the application layer.

sections.title: Addressing at each layer
sections.body:
Four kinds of address work together, and you need all of them, like the flat number, street, city and name on a letter. A port picks the process (transport). An IP address picks the host across networks (network). A MAC address picks the interface on one link (data link). And a name such as example.com is turned into an IP by DNS (application).

Here is a lovely detail. Along a route the IP addresses stay the same end to end, while the MAC addresses change at every hop. Which address is rewritten at every router along the path? The MAC address, because each link has its own.

questions.prompt: Which address is rewritten at every router along the path?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each hop is a new link with its own frame.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: They name processes and stay put.

problems.prompt: A host sends a packet to a server in another network. Which addresses change at the router and which stay the same?
problems.answer: Source and destination IP addresses stay the same (except with NAT); the frame’s MAC source and destination are rewritten at each hop because MAC addresses only mean something on one link.

keynotes: A port picks the process, an IP address picks the host across networks, a MAC address picks the interface on one link and a name is turned into an IP by DNS.
Along a route the IP addresses stay the same end to end.
MAC addresses change at every hop.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Three lines, and you have the map of the course.

  • Layers hide complexity; each talks to its peer via a protocol.
  • Going down, headers are added; going up, removed.
  • Hub → switch → router see layers 1 → 2 → 3.
keynotes: Layers hide complexity and each talks to its peer via a protocol.
Going down, headers are added; going up, they are removed.
Hub, switch and router see layers 1, 2 and 3 respectively.
